title: Cylinder 11 Misfire Detected
shortDescription: The PCM detected misfires in cylinder 11 on a high-displacement engine.
fullDescription:
P0311 is set when the PCM's crankshaft position monitoring detects repeated combustion events failing in cylinder 11. This code applies to engines with 12+ cylinders such as V12s found in luxury vehicles. Misfires reduce power, increase emissions, and can destroy the catalytic converter if left unresolved.

The issue typically stems from ignition coil, spark plug, fuel injector, or mechanical (compression) problems on that specific cylinder. On V12s with individual coil-on-plug systems, the coil is the most common culprit.
safetyImpact: Reduced power and rough running; continued driving can damage the catalytic converter.

causes.cause: Vacuum leak near cylinder 11 intake runner

fixSteps.title: Confirm code and swap test coil
fixSteps.instruction: Scan for active misfire counters, then swap the coil and plug from cylinder 11 with a neighboring cylinder. Clear codes and drive to see if the misfire follows.

fixSteps.title: Replace spark plug and coil if needed
fixSteps.instruction: Install new iridium/platinum plug and OEM ignition coil on cylinder 11.

fixSteps.title: Test injector and compression
fixSteps.instruction: If misfire persists, noid-light the injector and perform a compression test on cylinder 11.

faq.a: Only briefly. Flashing CEL means active misfire that can destroy the catalytic converter within hours.
Check the engine diagram in your service manual; cylinder numbering varies by manufacturer.

title: Cylinder 12 Misfire Detected
shortDescription: The PCM detected misfires in cylinder 12 on a V12 or similar high-cylinder engine.
fullDescription:
P0312 signals a persistent misfire on cylinder 12. The PCM uses crankshaft velocity deceleration between firing events to detect which cylinder is failing. This code is exclusive to engines with 12 or more cylinders (Mercedes, BMW, Audi, Rolls-Royce, Bentley, etc.).

Common root causes are ignition coil failure, fouled spark plug, clogged/dead fuel injector, or a mechanical compression issue. Given the cost of parts for V12 platforms, proper diagnosis before replacement is critical.
safetyImpact: Loss of power and potential catalytic converter damage if ignored.

fixSteps.title: Verify misfire counts
fixSteps.instruction: Read live data mode $06 misfire counters to confirm cylinder 12 is the offender.

fixSteps.title: Swap coils and plugs
fixSteps.instruction: Move the coil/plug from cyl 12 to another cylinder. If the misfire migrates, replace the defective part.

fixSteps.title: Check injector and compression
fixSteps.instruction: Noid light the injector circuit; if pulsing normally, perform compression and leak-down test on cyl 12.

faq.q: Is this a common code on V12s?
faq.a: Yes; coil failure on rear cylinders is very common due to heat exposure.

title: Misfire Detected with Low Fuel
shortDescription: Misfires are being detected while the fuel level is low.
fullDescription:
P0313 is set when the PCM detects multiple misfires and the fuel level is below a calibrated threshold (typically under 15%). This code exists because running a vehicle low on fuel can starve injectors, cavitate the fuel pump, and mimic other misfire conditions.

The primary recommended action is to refill the tank. If misfires continue after refueling, additional diagnosis for the real ignition/fuel cause is required.
safetyImpact: Engine may stall unexpectedly; potential fuel pump damage from repeated low-fuel operation.

causes.cause: Weak fuel pump unable to maintain pressure at low fuel

fixSteps.title: Refill fuel tank
fixSteps.instruction: Add at least half a tank of fresh fuel and drive a full drive cycle.

fixSteps.title: Clear codes and monitor
fixSteps.instruction: Clear DTCs and monitor with a scan tool to see if misfires return with adequate fuel.

fixSteps.title: Test fuel pressure
fixSteps.instruction: If misfires persist with full tank, check fuel pressure at the rail; replace pump or filter if below spec.

faq.q: Do I really just need gas?
faq.a: Often yes. Refuel and clear the code; if it returns with a full tank, diagnose further.

title: Single Cylinder Misfire (Cylinder Not Specified)
shortDescription: A misfire has been detected on a single cylinder, but the PCM cannot identify which one.
fullDescription:
P0314 is set when the PCM detects a misfire pattern consistent with a single cylinder but cannot determine which cylinder is misfiring. This often happens when the crankshaft/camshaft correlation is off, or when the misfire is intermittent and only the rough-running flag trips without positive identification.

Common causes include ignition, fuel delivery, compression, or CKP/CMP sensor issues that prevent misfire attribution.
safetyImpact: Reduced power and potential converter damage if misfire is severe.

causes.cause: Faulty ignition coil or plug on an unknown cylinder

fixSteps.title: Check CKP/CMP signals
fixSteps.instruction: Scope the crankshaft and camshaft sensors to ensure clean signals with no missing teeth.

fixSteps.title: Inspect tune-up parts
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect all spark plugs and coils; replace anything worn.

fixSteps.title: Compression test
fixSteps.instruction: Perform a compression check on all cylinders to find outliers.

faq.q: Why can't the PCM tell which cylinder?
faq.a: Misfire attribution requires accurate CKP/CMP timing; intermittent signals or weak misfires can prevent identification.

title: Misfire Detected on Startup (First 1000 Revolutions)
shortDescription: A misfire was detected during the first 1000 engine revolutions after startup.
fullDescription:
P0316 is a Ford-specific OBD-II code (also used by some other makes) that indicates the PCM detected misfires during the first 1000 revolutions of engine operation after a cold start. This is a precursor code — usually a P0300-series code will also set identifying the specific cylinder.

The code exists because cold-start misfires are often diagnostic of fuel injector, compression, or valve-seat issues that only manifest briefly on startup.
safetyImpact: Extended misfiring can overheat and damage the catalytic converter.

causes.cause: Valve seat recession (common on some Ford 5.4L Triton engines)

symptoms: Rough idle for first few seconds

fixSteps.title: Read accompanying misfire codes
fixSteps.instruction: Note any P0301-P0310 codes; they identify the affected cylinder.

fixSteps.title: Inspect spark plugs and coils
fixSteps.instruction: Replace plugs at the specified interval; swap-test coils if needed.

fixSteps.title: Perform wet/dry compression test
fixSteps.instruction: Test each cylinder cold; low readings indicate valve or ring problems.

faq.q: Is P0316 serious on my 5.4L Ford?
faq.a: Possibly. On some Triton engines it can indicate valve-seat issues requiring head work.

title: Rough Road Hardware Not Present
shortDescription: The PCM expected a rough-road sensor input but none is detected.
fullDescription:
P0317 indicates the PCM's misfire detection strategy expected to receive a rough-road signal (typically from the ABS wheel speed sensors or a dedicated G-sensor) to compensate for false misfires caused by rough pavement, but the signal is not available.

On rough roads, crankshaft speed can fluctuate enough to mimic misfires. The rough-road input filters these false signals. Missing data usually indicates an ABS module fault or wiring issue between modules.
safetyImpact: Minimal direct impact; may cause false misfire codes on rough roads.

causes.cause: Wiring/CAN bus issue between ABS and PCM
Missing or failed wheel speed sensor

symptoms: Other false misfire codes setting on rough roads

fixSteps.title: Scan ABS module
fixSteps.instruction: Check for ABS DTCs and repair those first.

fixSteps.title: Verify CAN communication
fixSteps.instruction: Use a scan tool to verify ABS and PCM are communicating over the network.

fixSteps.title: PCM software update
fixSteps.instruction: Check for TSB/calibration updates from the manufacturer.

faq.a: Not directly. It mainly affects misfire detection reliability.

title: Rough Road Sensor A Signal Circuit
shortDescription: Fault detected in the rough-road sensor A signal circuit.
fullDescription:
P0318 sets when the PCM detects an out-of-range or erratic signal from the rough-road sensor A — either a G-sensor or the ABS-derived wheel speed signal used for misfire filtering. The signal is either missing, stuck, or implausible.

This code often accompanies false misfire DTCs because the PCM cannot filter out crankshaft velocity noise caused by bumpy roads.
safetyImpact: Minor; false misfire codes may set on rough pavement.

causes.cause: Failed G-sensor or wheel speed sensor

fixSteps.title: Locate the sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Reference service info to find the rough-road sensor (often integrated with ABS).

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring and connectors
fixSteps.instruction: Check for damage, corrosion, and verify signal voltage with a multimeter.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor if faulty
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor and clear codes.

faq.a: A sensor that detects road roughness so the PCM can filter out false misfires.

title: Rough Road Sensor B Signal Circuit
shortDescription: Fault detected in the rough-road sensor B signal circuit.
fullDescription:
P0319 is similar to P0318 but refers to the B circuit of the rough-road sensor system. On some vehicles, two signals (A and B) from different sources are compared for plausibility.

The code indicates missing, erratic, or out-of-range signal from the B input. Common causes mirror those of P0318: sensor, wiring, or module issues.
safetyImpact: Minor; may cause false misfire codes.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect harness to sensor B.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new rough-road sensor B if wiring is good.

faq.a: Yes, but you may see other misfire codes appear spuriously.

title: Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit No Signal
shortDescription: No RPM signal detected from the ignition/distributor input circuit.
fullDescription:
P0322 is set when the PCM detects no signal at all from the engine speed input circuit connected to the ignition system or distributor. On older vehicles this is the pickup coil in the distributor; on newer vehicles it may be a dedicated ignition module input.

Without this signal the engine will not start or will stall. The code usually points to a pickup coil, CKP sensor, module, or wiring failure.
safetyImpact: Engine may not start or may stall while driving.

causes.cause: Failed distributor pickup coil or ignition module
Broken wiring between ignition and PCM
Failed CKP sensor on distributor-less systems

fixSteps.title: Scope the signal
fixSteps.instruction: Use an oscilloscope to check for AC signal from the pickup or CKP while cranking.

fixSteps.title: Replace pickup/CKP
fixSteps.instruction: Replace faulty pickup coil or crankshaft sensor as identified.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Continuity-test the harness from the sensor to the PCM.

faq.a: Usually no; without an RPM input the PCM will not fire injectors/coils.

title: Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit Intermittent
shortDescription: Intermittent signal from the ignition/distributor engine speed input.
fullDescription:
P0323 indicates the PCM saw the RPM input signal drop out intermittently. Unlike P0322 (no signal), the signal is present sometimes but cuts out. This often results in intermittent stalling, hard starting, or tach needle dropping to zero while driving.

Vibration-sensitive wiring, a failing pickup coil, or a cracked reluctor ring are typical culprits.

causes.cause: Failing pickup coil or CKP sensor

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test
fixSteps.instruction: With engine running, wiggle the pickup/CKP connector while watching for stalls.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace pickup coil or CKP sensor.

fixSteps.title: Repair wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Repair any damaged wires or connectors.

faq.a: Heat and vibration often cause wiring or sensor elements to open momentarily.

title: Knock Control System Error
shortDescription: The knock sensor control module has detected an internal error.
fullDescription:
P0324 is set when the knock control subsystem (either an external knock control module or the internal PCM module) reports a general error preventing proper knock monitoring. This code can set due to a bad knock sensor, module failure, or wiring issue.

Knock sensors detect engine detonation and allow the PCM to retard timing to prevent damage. With the knock system disabled, the PCM will often run a conservative timing map which reduces power and fuel economy.
safetyImpact: Engine may run with retarded timing; severe knock could damage engine.

fixSteps.title: Scan and inspect
fixSteps.instruction: Check for related P0325-P0334 codes.

fixSteps.title: Test knock sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Measure sensor resistance and inspect wiring.

fixSteps.title: Replace module/sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the knock sensor or module as indicated.

faq.a: Short-term yes, but avoid heavy loads and premium-only fuel requirements.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Circuit Low Input (Bank 1)
shortDescription: Signal voltage from knock sensor 1 is below the expected range.
fullDescription:
P0327 indicates the PCM measured a knock sensor 1 signal below the minimum threshold — effectively the sensor is not producing enough voltage. This is a very common code, especially on GM 4.8/5.3/6.0 V8 engines where knock sensors live under the intake manifold and fail from corrosion.

Other causes include a short to ground in the signal wire, improper torque, or a failed PCM input.
safetyImpact: PCM retards timing defensively; mild power and economy loss.

causes.cause: Short to ground in signal wire

fixSteps.title: Inspect sensor location
fixSteps.instruction: On many V8s, remove the intake manifold to access bank 1 knock sensor.

fixSteps.title: Replace knock sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor torqued to spec (~15 ft-lb typical).

fixSteps.title: Update wiring harness
fixSteps.instruction: Many GM trucks benefit from the updated knock sensor harness.

faq.q: Why is this code common on GM V8s?
faq.a: Sensors sit in valley under intake; coolant and condensation corrode them.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Circuit High Input (Bank 1)
shortDescription: Signal voltage from knock sensor 1 is above the expected range.
fullDescription:
P0328 sets when the PCM sees higher-than-spec voltage on the knock sensor 1 circuit (bank 1). This can be caused by a short to voltage, a failed sensor outputting excessive noise, or a wiring fault.

When knock input is out of range, the PCM ignores actual knock events and may retard timing preemptively.
safetyImpact: Possible loss of power; risk of undetected knock damage.

causes.cause: Short to voltage in signal wire
Failed knock sensor producing erratic output

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect signal wire for shorts to nearby voltage sources.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace knock sensor with proper torque.

faq.q: Low vs high input — same fix?
faq.a: Often yes; the sensor or wiring is the root in both cases.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Circuit Low Input (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Signal voltage from knock sensor 2 is below the expected range.
fullDescription:
P0332 is the bank 2 counterpart to P0327. Many V6 and V8 engines use two knock sensors, one per cylinder bank. When the bank 2 sensor produces insufficient signal, P0332 sets and the PCM loses knock monitoring on that bank.

Causes include sensor failure, wiring short to ground, or improper installation torque.
safetyImpact: Timing retarded on bank 2; mild power loss.

causes.cause: Short to ground in signal wire

fixSteps.title: Access sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Locate bank 2 knock sensor (typically on the opposite bank from bank 1).

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor torqued to specification.

faq.a: Often recommended since both sensors are the same age.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Circuit High Input (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Signal voltage from knock sensor 2 is above the expected range.
fullDescription: P0333 sets when bank 2 knock sensor signal is higher than allowed. This can indicate a short to voltage, a failing sensor producing excessive noise, or loose mounting generating mechanical vibration artifacts.
safetyImpact: Reduced power on bank 2 side; potential undetected knock.

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check for short to voltage or damaged insulation.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new bank 2 knock sensor.

faq.a: Quality aftermarket sensors are fine; avoid very cheap ones that fail quickly.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)
shortDescription: The bank 2 knock sensor 2 signal is intermittent.
fullDescription:
P0334 indicates the PCM has seen intermittent dropouts or spikes from knock sensor 2 on bank 2. Rather than a steady high or low fault, the signal comes and goes — typically caused by wiring issues, loose connectors, or a sensor beginning to fail.

Left alone, the code may progress to P0332 or P0333 as the fault becomes permanent.
safetyImpact: Occasional loss of knock monitoring; minor power impact.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test
fixSteps.instruction: Wiggle sensor connector while monitoring live data.

fixSteps.title: Repair wiring or replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Repair connector issues or install a new sensor.

faq.a: Yes, dielectric grease on a cleaned connector often resolves intermittent issues.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Low Input (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Camshaft sensor A on bank 2 reads below expected voltage.
fullDescription:
P0347 indicates the PCM detects camshaft position sensor A on bank 2 producing a signal below the minimum voltage threshold. A constant low voltage can result from a shorted-to-ground signal wire, failed sensor, or loss of reference voltage from the PCM.

On engines with variable valve timing, a missing camshaft signal often disables VVT and can cause hard starting and rough running.
safetyImpact: Reduced power; engine may stall or be hard to start.

causes.cause: Short to ground in signal wire

fixSteps.title: Check signal and power
fixSteps.instruction: Back-probe sensor connector and verify 5V reference and clean AC/digital signal.

fixSteps.title: Replace CMP sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor on bank 2 camshaft.

fixSteps.title: Repair wiring
fixSteps.instruction: If wiring shorted, repair or replace the harness segment.

faq.q: What is sensor A vs B?
faq.a: Some engines have multiple cam sensors; A typically refers to intake cam, B to exhaust cam.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit High Input (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Camshaft sensor A on bank 2 reads above expected voltage.
fullDescription: P0348 is set when the PCM detects bank 2 camshaft sensor A output above the upper voltage threshold. Possible causes are a short to voltage, a failed sensor, or a wiring issue putting unintended voltage on the signal line.
safetyImpact: VVT may disable; reduced power and potential hard starts.

causes.cause: Short to voltage on signal wire

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect harness for short to voltage.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CMP sensor bank 2.

faq.q: Could the PCM be at fault?
faq.a: Rarely, but possible. Rule out wiring and sensor first.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Intermittent signal from bank 2 camshaft sensor A.
fullDescription: P0349 sets when the PCM sees the bank 2 camshaft sensor A signal drop out or spike intermittently. This often correlates with heat, vibration, or marginal connections. Intermittent faults eventually become permanent, so early investigation is wise.
safetyImpact: Possible intermittent rough running or stalling.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test connector
fixSteps.instruction: Gently move harness while engine runs to reproduce dropout.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CMP sensor.

faq.q: Can I just clear the code?
faq.a: It will return; replacement is the reliable fix.

title: Ignition Coil A Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil A's primary or secondary circuit.
fullDescription:
P0351 indicates the PCM detected an electrical fault in ignition coil A (usually the coil for cylinder 1 on coil-on-plug systems, or the first coil pack on DIS systems). The issue can be on the primary side (PCM-driven low voltage) or secondary (high-voltage output to spark plug).

Common causes are a failed coil, open/shorted primary winding, damaged wiring, or a PCM driver circuit failure.
safetyImpact: Misfire on cylinder 1; catalytic converter at risk if prolonged.

fixSteps.title: Swap test
fixSteps.instruction: Swap coil A with another cylinder's coil; if code follows, replace the coil.

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check harness and connector for damage.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM-quality ignition coil.

faq.a: Typically cylinder 1, but verify with service info for your vehicle.

title: Ignition Coil B Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil B's primary or secondary circuit.
fullDescription: P0352 indicates a fault on ignition coil B — typically cylinder 2 in COP systems. Similar diagnosis applies as P0351: inspect the coil, wiring, connector, and PCM driver.

fixSteps.title: Swap-test coil
fixSteps.instruction: Exchange with known-good coil and clear codes.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil B
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM-spec ignition coil.

faq.a: If multiple are original and high-mileage, replacing all is reasonable preventive work.

title: Ignition Coil C Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil C.
fullDescription: P0353 is set for ignition coil C (typically cylinder 3). The code results from an electrical fault in the primary or secondary windings, wiring, or PCM driver. Diagnosis and repair follow the same pattern as coils A and B.

fixSteps.title: Swap and test
fixSteps.instruction: Swap coil C with another; verify fault migrates.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM-quality coil.

faq.a: Heat, vibration, oil contamination, and age all degrade coil windings.

title: Ignition Coil D Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil D.
fullDescription: P0354 refers to ignition coil D, typically cylinder 4. Same pattern as prior coil codes: swap test, inspect wiring, replace coil if confirmed faulty.

fixSteps.title: Swap test
fixSteps.instruction: Swap with known-good coil to confirm.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM-spec coil.

faq.q: Do I need a new plug too?
faq.a: It's good practice to replace the plug at the same time as the coil.

title: Ignition Coil E Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil E.
fullDescription: P0355 refers to ignition coil E, typically cylinder 5. V6, V8, or inline-5 engines will have a coil E. Causes mirror other coil codes: primary winding open/short, secondary fault, wiring, or PCM driver issue.

fixSteps.title: Swap and verify
fixSteps.instruction: Swap coil E with another and retest.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new coil.

faq.a: Rear-bank coils on transverse V6s may require removing intake or cover.

title: Ignition Coil F Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil F.
fullDescription: P0356 is the coil F code — cylinder 6. Applies to V6, V8, inline-6 engines. Same diagnostic path: swap test, inspect wiring, replace if confirmed.

fixSteps.title: Swap test
fixSteps.instruction: Verify fault follows the coil.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM-quality coil.

faq.a: Typically 80,000-150,000 miles; heat and age shorten life.

title: Ignition Coil G Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil G.
fullDescription: P0357 refers to ignition coil G (cylinder 7). Applies to V8, V10, and V12 engines. Diagnostic process identical to earlier coil codes.

fixSteps.title: Swap test
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm by swapping with known-good coil.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new coil.

faq.a: OEM coils usually have better longevity; brand-name aftermarket is acceptable.

title: Ignition Coil H Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil H.
fullDescription: P0358 refers to coil H — cylinder 8, common on V8 engines. Same diagnostic steps apply; swap testing is quickest.

fixSteps.title: Swap and test
fixSteps.instruction: Swap with another cylinder's coil and recheck.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new coil.

faq.a: Replace any plug with excessive wear; it's cheap insurance.

title: Ignition Coil I Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil I.
fullDescription: P0359 refers to coil I (cylinder 9) on V10 or V12 engines. Rare code — most consumer engines don't have a coil I. Diagnostic pattern unchanged.

fixSteps.title: Swap coils
fixSteps.instruction: Move coil I to another position; see if fault follows.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM coil.

faq.a: V10s (Dodge Viper, Audi R8/S6/S8) and V12s.

title: Ignition Coil J Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil J.
fullDescription: P0360 refers to coil J — cylinder 10 on V10 engines. Same standard diagnostic approach; often associated with luxury/exotic V10/V12 platforms where each coil is expensive.

fixSteps.title: Swap test
fixSteps.instruction: Swap coil J with another and retest.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM coil.

faq.a: OEM coils on exotics can run $150-300 each.

title: Ignition Coil K Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil K.
fullDescription: P0361 refers to ignition coil K (cylinder 11) on V12 engines. Same diagnostic steps — swap test first.

fixSteps.title: Swap test
fixSteps.instruction: Swap with adjacent coil.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new coil.

faq.a: Rear bank coils often require intake or cowl removal.

title: Ignition Coil L Primary/Secondary Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The PCM detected a fault in ignition coil L.
fullDescription: P0362 refers to coil L (cylinder 12) — V12 engines only. Standard coil diagnosis and replacement.

fixSteps.title: Swap test
fixSteps.instruction: Verify fault via coil swap.

fixSteps.title: Replace coil
fixSteps.instruction: Install new OEM coil.

faq.q: Should I replace all V12 coils?
faq.a: If original and high-mileage, doing all 12 is sensible preventive maintenance.

title: Misfire Detected - Fuel Shut Off
shortDescription: The PCM has detected excessive misfiring and shut off fuel to protect the catalytic converter.
fullDescription:
P0363 is set when the PCM's misfire protection strategy determines that continued fuel delivery to a misfiring cylinder would damage the catalytic converter. The PCM cuts injector pulse to the affected cylinder and sets this code alongside a P030x.

This is a protective measure; the real problem is whatever's causing the misfire. Fix the root cause (coil, plug, injector, compression) and fuel will be restored.
safetyImpact: Vehicle drivable but with reduced power and severe misfire; limp behavior possible.

fixSteps.title: Diagnose misfire code
fixSteps.instruction: Read paired P030x code to identify affected cylinder.

fixSteps.title: Repair underlying fault
fixSteps.instruction: Replace coil, plug, injector, or address compression issue.

fixSteps.title: Clear codes
fixSteps.instruction: Clear codes and drive to verify fuel is restored.

faq.a: Yes, to that specific cylinder — a protective measure until the misfire is resolved.

title: Ignition Coil Reserved (Manufacturer Specific)
shortDescription: Reserved ignition coil code — manufacturer-specific usage.
fullDescription: P0364 is reserved in the OBD-II spec and used differently across manufacturers. Some OEMs use it as a generic ignition coil control circuit fault; others for additional coil diagnostics. Refer to vehicle-specific service information.

fixSteps.title: Consult service info
fixSteps.instruction: Look up manufacturer definition of P0364 for your vehicle.

fixSteps.title: Perform directed test
fixSteps.instruction: Follow OEM diagnostic procedure.

faq.a: Yes, but the meaning depends on your vehicle's OEM.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit (Bank 1)
shortDescription: A general fault with camshaft position sensor B on bank 1.
fullDescription: P0365 is set when the PCM detects a circuit fault with camshaft position sensor B on bank 1. In engines with dual cam phasers (intake and exhaust), sensor B typically monitors the exhaust cam. Loss of this sensor disables exhaust VVT functionality.
safetyImpact: Loss of VVT on exhaust cam; reduced power and efficiency.

fixSteps.title: Locate sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Find CMP sensor B on bank 1 — usually on the exhaust cam housing.

fixSteps.title: Test and replace
fixSteps.instruction: Verify sensor signal with scope, then replace if bad.

faq.a: The sensor for it is; the actuator may still be fine.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
shortDescription: Bank 1 CMP sensor B is producing an implausible signal.
fullDescription: P0366 sets when the camshaft position sensor B (bank 1) signal is out of expected range relative to the crankshaft position — the timing relationship is off or the signal is erratic. Causes include reluctor damage, timing chain stretch, or sensor failure.
safetyImpact: Rough running, reduced power, possible misfires.

fixSteps.title: Check timing with scan data
fixSteps.instruction: View CMP/CKP correlation data; deviation indicates chain or phaser issue.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor first
fixSteps.instruction: If data is erratic, try sensor first.

fixSteps.title: Inspect timing components
fixSteps.instruction: If correlation is consistently off, inspect chain and tensioners.

faq.q: Could it be the timing chain?
faq.a: Yes — stretched chains are a common cause on higher-mileage direct-injection engines.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Input (Bank 1)
shortDescription: CMP sensor B bank 1 signal is below minimum voltage.
fullDescription: P0367 sets when CMP sensor B on bank 1 outputs a signal below the minimum voltage threshold. Similar to P0347 but for the B sensor (exhaust cam). Causes include short to ground, sensor failure, or loss of reference voltage.

fixSteps.title: Measure sensor voltage
fixSteps.instruction: Check reference voltage and signal with DMM.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CMP sensor.

faq.q: Do I need to relearn anything?
faq.a: Usually no, but some OEMs require a cam relearn after sensor replacement.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High Input (Bank 1)
shortDescription: CMP sensor B bank 1 signal is above maximum voltage.
fullDescription: P0368 sets when CMP sensor B on bank 1 outputs above the expected maximum. Typical causes are a short to voltage, failed sensor, or wiring damage. VVT will typically default to a base position.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect harness for shorts to 12V or 5V reference.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CMP sensor.

faq.a: Not immediately, but the car will run less efficiently.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1)
shortDescription: Intermittent signal on CMP sensor B bank 1.
fullDescription: P0369 indicates the CMP sensor B bank 1 signal has intermittent dropouts. This is usually caused by heat-sensitive wiring or a marginally failing sensor. Not immediately critical but will progress to a hard fault.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test
fixSteps.instruction: Reproduce dropout by wiggling harness.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor, clean connector.

faq.a: Usually yes; intermittent codes generally become permanent over time.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A Malfunction
shortDescription: High-resolution timing reference signal A malfunction.
fullDescription:
P0370 sets when the PCM detects a fault in the high-resolution timing signal used for precise fuel and spark control, often seen on diesel engines with high-resolution crank sensing. The signal can be missing, intermittent, or out of range.

Diesel injection precision relies on this signal; loss of it causes rough running and reduced power.
safetyImpact: Significant power loss; diesel may stall.

fixSteps.title: Scope CKP signal
fixSteps.instruction: Verify clean pattern with no missing teeth.

fixSteps.title: Replace CKP
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor.

fixSteps.title: Inspect tone ring
fixSteps.instruction: Check for damage or debris.

faq.a: Most common on diesel engines with precision timing requirements.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A Too Many Pulses
shortDescription: Too many pulses detected on the high-resolution timing signal A.
fullDescription: P0371 sets when the PCM receives more pulses per revolution than expected on the high-resolution timing signal A. Causes include electrical interference, a damaged reluctor with extra teeth, or wiring picking up noise from other sources.

causes.cause: Electrical noise from alternator or ignition
Wiring routed too close to high-voltage source

fixSteps.title: Scope signal
fixSteps.instruction: Look for extra transitions or noise on scope.

fixSteps.title: Inspect and replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace sensor and verify wiring routing.

faq.a: A failing alternator with ripple can induce noise on sensor lines.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A Too Few Pulses
shortDescription: Fewer pulses than expected on high-resolution timing signal A.
fullDescription: P0372 indicates the PCM is receiving fewer pulses than expected per crank revolution on the high-resolution timing signal. Often points to a damaged or chipped reluctor tooth, failing sensor, or wiring fault causing signal dropout.

fixSteps.title: Inspect reluctor
fixSteps.instruction: Visually inspect for missing/damaged teeth.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CKP with correct air gap.

faq.a: Often it's pressed onto the crank; may require significant engine disassembly.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A Intermittent/Erratic Pulses
shortDescription: Intermittent or erratic pulses on high-resolution timing signal A.
fullDescription: P0373 sets when the high-resolution timing signal A shows irregular or intermittent pulse patterns. Unlike P0371/P0372 which describe too many/too few pulses, this code covers erratic patterns that don't fit the steady-state high/low failure modes.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test
fixSteps.instruction: Look for signal dropouts while moving harness.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor and harness as needed
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor; repair wiring.

faq.a: Heat cycling and vibration weaken solder joints and sensor windings over time.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A No Pulses
shortDescription: No pulses detected on high-resolution timing signal A.
fullDescription: P0374 sets when the PCM receives zero high-resolution timing pulses. This generally results in a no-start or immediate stall condition since precision timing is unavailable. Usually caused by a complete sensor failure, broken wire, or severely damaged reluctor.
safetyImpact: No start or stall while driving.

fixSteps.title: Check for sensor signal
fixSteps.instruction: Scope during cranking to verify any output.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CKP.

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Continuity test harness to PCM.

faq.a: Usually no until the fault is resolved.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal B Malfunction
shortDescription: High-resolution timing reference signal B malfunction.
fullDescription: P0375 is the B-circuit counterpart to P0370. Some engines use two high-resolution timing signals for redundancy or to cover different functions. A fault on signal B produces similar symptoms.

fixSteps.title: Scope signal B
fixSteps.instruction: Verify signal presence and integrity.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor on signal B circuit.

faq.a: Mainly on high-end or diesel applications with redundant timing.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal B Too Many Pulses
shortDescription: Too many pulses on high-resolution timing signal B.
fullDescription: P0376 mirrors P0371 but for signal B — too many pulses counted per revolution. Similar causes: noise, reluctor damage, sensor fault.

fixSteps.title: Scope signal
fixSteps.instruction: Identify source of extra pulses.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor/repair wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the sensor and route wiring away from noise sources.

faq.q: Can spark plug wires cause this?
faq.a: Yes, arcing plug wires induce noise on nearby signal lines.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal B Too Few Pulses
shortDescription: Fewer than expected pulses on high-resolution timing signal B.
fullDescription: P0377 indicates too few pulses from high-resolution signal B. Analogous to P0372. Usually sensor, air gap, or reluctor damage.

fixSteps.title: Inspect reluctor and sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Check for tooth damage and air gap.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor.

faq.a: Just a sensor if the reluctor is okay; reluctor replacement is costly.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal B Intermittent/Erratic
shortDescription: Intermittent signal B pulses detected.
fullDescription: P0378 indicates erratic or intermittent pulse pattern on timing reference signal B. Similar troubleshooting as P0373.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test
fixSteps.instruction: Try to reproduce fault with harness movement.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor and repair wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor and fix any harness issues.

faq.a: No, they should be diagnosed before progressing to hard failures.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal B No Pulses
shortDescription: No pulses detected on timing reference signal B.
fullDescription: P0379 is set when signal B is completely absent. Engine may run on signal A alone in degraded mode, or refuse to start depending on system architecture.
safetyImpact: Major performance loss or no start.

fixSteps.title: Scope and continuity test
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm zero signal; test harness continuity.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor.

faq.a: Likely yes — car may be immobile until fixed.

title: Glow Plug/Heater Circuit A Malfunction
shortDescription: A fault in the diesel glow plug heater circuit A.
fullDescription: P0380 is a diesel-specific code indicating the PCM/ECM detected a fault in the glow plug heater circuit A. Glow plugs preheat combustion chambers for reliable cold starts on diesel engines. The code may point to a failed plug, glow plug relay/control module, or wiring fault.
safetyImpact: Hard cold starts; engine may not start at all below freezing.
symptoms: Wait-to-start light stays on too long

fixSteps.title: Test each glow plug
fixSteps.instruction: Measure resistance of each glow plug; bad ones read open or far from spec.

fixSteps.title: Test glow plug relay/module
fixSteps.instruction: Verify voltage supply to plugs during preheat cycle.

fixSteps.title: Replace faulty components
fixSteps.instruction: Replace all glow plugs and controller if needed.

faq.a: Yes, recommended — they age together.

title: Glow Plug Indicator Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: A fault in the glow plug indicator (wait-to-start lamp) circuit.
fullDescription: P0381 indicates a fault specifically in the dashboard wait-to-start indicator circuit — the lamp that tells the driver glow plugs are active. Can be bulb, wiring, or instrument cluster issue.
safetyImpact: Minor; driver may not see preheat indication.

fixSteps.title: Check bulb
fixSteps.instruction: Replace indicator bulb if burnt.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Test circuit from cluster to ECM.

faq.q: Is the glow plug system working?
faq.a: Often yes — this is just the lamp.

title: Glow Plug/Heater Circuit B Malfunction
shortDescription: A fault in glow plug circuit B.
fullDescription: P0383 applies to glow plug circuit B on diesel engines with multiple glow plug circuits (typically V6/V8 diesels with one circuit per bank). Same troubleshooting as P0380.

causes.cause: Failed glow plugs on circuit B

fixSteps.title: Test bank B plugs
fixSteps.instruction: Resistance check each glow plug.

fixSteps.title: Replace plugs and/or controller
fixSteps.instruction: Install new components.

faq.a: Passenger or driver bank depending on vehicle layout — check service info.

title: Glow Plug/Heater Circuit B Range/Performance
shortDescription: Glow plug circuit B current draw is out of specification.
fullDescription: P0384 is set when the current on glow plug circuit B is outside the expected range — either too high (short) or too low (one or more plugs open). The ECM monitors current during preheat cycles.

causes.cause: One or more bad glow plugs

fixSteps.title: Measure each plug's resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Identify any open or shorted plug.

fixSteps.title: Replace faulty plugs
fixSteps.instruction: Install new glow plugs as a set.

faq.a: All together — matched age improves reliability.

title: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
shortDescription: CKP sensor B signal is out of expected range.
fullDescription: P0386 indicates the PCM detects CKP sensor B signal is present but not within plausible range. Common on engines with dual crank sensors for redundancy. The signal may be consistently high/low, or the timing relationship with sensor A is off.

fixSteps.title: Scope signal
fixSteps.instruction: Compare A and B patterns for correct relationship.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CKP sensor B.

faq.q: Both A and B sensors needed?
faq.a: Yes, some systems require both for full function.

title: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Input
shortDescription: CKP sensor B signal voltage is below minimum.
fullDescription: P0387 sets when the PCM sees CKP B signal voltage below expected minimum. Typical causes are short to ground, failed sensor, or open reference voltage.

fixSteps.title: Measure signal
fixSteps.instruction: Check voltage during cranking.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor/fix wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Replace CKP or repair harness.

faq.q: Car runs poorly or not at all?
faq.a: Usually no start or intermittent stall.

title: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High Input
shortDescription: CKP sensor B signal voltage is above maximum.
fullDescription: P0388 sets when the PCM sees CKP B signal voltage above the upper threshold. Causes include short to voltage or a malfunctioning sensor generating excessive output.

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Look for shorts to 12V/5V sources.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor.

faq.a: Short to voltage can be harder to trace; inspect bundled wiring carefully.

title: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
shortDescription: Intermittent CKP sensor B signal.
fullDescription: P0389 indicates CKP B signal has intermittent dropouts. Typically progresses to a hard failure. Address promptly to avoid getting stranded.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle/heat test
fixSteps.instruction: Try to reproduce dropout with harness movement or heat gun near sensor.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new CKP.

faq.a: Yes, intermittent CKP faults are notorious for progressing to no-start.

title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The fuel composition (flex-fuel) sensor circuit has a fault.
fullDescription: P0176 sets when the PCM detects a general malfunction in the fuel composition sensor circuit. On flex-fuel vehicles, this sensor measures ethanol content of the fuel so the PCM can adjust fueling and timing. Without this data, the engine defaults to a safe calibration, typically losing some power and efficiency.
safetyImpact: Reduced power; engine defaults to conservative calibration.

fixSteps.title: Locate sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Find flex-fuel sensor (usually inline on the fuel feed line).

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check connector and harness.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new flex-fuel sensor, relieve fuel pressure first.

faq.a: Switch to gasoline until repaired; PCM may not correctly compensate for E85.

title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Low Input
shortDescription: Flex-fuel sensor signal is below expected minimum.
fullDescription: P0178 indicates the flex-fuel sensor signal is below the minimum threshold. Usually a short to ground, failed sensor, or loss of reference voltage.

fixSteps.title: Check sensor voltage
fixSteps.instruction: Verify reference and signal voltages with DMM.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new flex-fuel sensor.

faq.a: Yes, the fuel is fine — the sensor just can't measure it correctly.

title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit High Input
shortDescription: Flex-fuel sensor signal is above expected maximum.
fullDescription: P0179 indicates the flex-fuel sensor signal is above maximum allowed. Causes: short to voltage, sensor failure, wiring damage.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring for shorts
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect harness near sensor.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new sensor.

faq.a: Not recommended — PCM still needs to know fuel composition on flex-fuel vehicles.

title: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: General fault in fuel temperature sensor A circuit.
fullDescription: P0180 sets when the PCM detects a general fault in the fuel temperature sensor A circuit. This sensor measures fuel temperature, which affects density and therefore injector pulse compensation, especially in diesel and flex-fuel applications.
safetyImpact: Minor driveability impact; fueling may be slightly off at temperature extremes.

fixSteps.title: Test sensor resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Check sensor per service manual spec at measured temperatures.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Install new fuel temperature sensor.

faq.a: No, fuel runs mostly okay with default temperature assumption.

title: OBD-II Monitor Testing Not Complete
shortDescription: The on-board diagnostic monitors have not all run to completion.
fullDescription:
P1000 is a Ford-specific code (and used similarly by Jaguar, Mazda) that indicates the OBD-II readiness monitors have not yet completed a full drive cycle. It is not a fault in the usual sense — it sets after the battery is disconnected, codes are cleared, or the PCM is reset, and the car hasn't yet completed the drive pattern needed to run all self-tests.

The car will usually pass emissions testing only after P1000 clears, which happens after a specific drive cycle is completed.

causes.cause: Recent battery disconnect or code clear

fixSteps.title: Perform Ford drive cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Follow the manufacturer drive cycle: warm-up, highway, and city segments.

fixSteps.title: Recheck readiness
fixSteps.instruction: Scan tool to confirm all monitors are Ready and P1000 has cleared.

faq.a: No — just drive it through a normal mix of driving to complete monitors.
